findings.issue: restore_copy can write over newer work at a path the copy holds. It drops every path in `held` from `_newer_work`'s answer (`[p for p in _newer_work(...) if p not in held]`), and `_undo` then `_put`s each held path unconditionally. Suppose a.txt is a held work path and, after the kill, someone (a human, or a writer session that was already running) edits it to bytes that are neither the copy's nor `start`'s nor `end`'s. The restore overwrites that edit without saying so. un7 covers only an unheld path (c.txt), so this direction has no test. The docstring narrows the contract to 'the paths it holds are what a restore is asked to write over', which conflicts with 'never write over newer work'.
findings.resolution: Before `_undo`, refuse any held path whose bytes match none of these: the copy (`_holds(tree, rel, held[rel])`), `start`'s blob, or `end`'s blob (`_reads_as`, absent where the commit has none). Those are the only states a killed move or a killed undo can leave. un6's tree (a.txt at base, n.txt absent) still passes. Add a case like un7 that edits a.txt and expects a refusal with nothing changed.

findings.issue: `hash-object --no-filters` costs more than the docstring says. With core.autocrlf=true, the Git for Windows installer default, every text file checkout writes with CRLF hashes differently from its LF blob. So a move killed partway through its checkout leaves moved paths that `_newer_work` reads as newer work. The resume holds the tree, and so does the restore verb the new stop names: restore_copy runs the same `_newer_work` and refuses those paths, because moved paths are not in `held`. On a default Windows checkout, the stop's sentence '`restore` puts the work back from it and takes it down' is then false and no verb can settle the tree. The filtered hash this replaces accepted those files.
findings.resolution: Compare the file's raw bytes with what checkout itself would write, `git cat-file --filters <commit>:<rel>` (smudge and EOL conversion applied under this tree's attributes and config). That rejects a file whose only change is its line endings and still accepts a CRLF checkout. Add a variant of un5 that sets core.autocrlf=true, checks out the head, and expects the file to read as the commit's.

findings.issue: The diff writes that `tree_unsettled` is 'the one reading every verb that touches a task tree takes first' and that 'a verb that dispatches into a task tree, integrates it, retires it or moves it asks tree_unsettled first'. The code does not hold that. (a) manage-worktrees.py:700-746 `task-remove` (the `/audit:worktree task-remove` remover of a task tree) never asks. It is not only `--force`, as the executor's outcome says: after a move killed inside its undo, the forced checkout leaves the tree clean, so even the unforced remove passes the dirtiness check, and `git worktree remove` then deletes the admin directory holding the only copy of the work. audit-status.py:2131/2135 prints that remover as the remedy for a kept tree, and retire_member now keeps exactly those trees. (b) drive-phase.py:2223-2250 `resume_writer` opens a writer session in the task tree through `open_dispatch` without going through `dispatch()`, so it never asks either. That path is only reachable if a copy appears after a gate-red-writer decision was parked.
findings.resolution: Either make the claim true by having manage-worktrees `task-remove` ask `_worktrees.tree_unsettled` and refuse anything but False, forced or not, naming the copy and the restore verb, and by routing `resume_writer` through `unsettled_stop`. Or narrow both sentences to the drive's own dispatch, integration, retirement and move, and file task-remove as a fault. Prefer the first, since the copy is the only record of the work.

findings.issue: Two refusals tell the user that 'the next move drops it': a copy with no index.json, and a copy of a move the marker already recorded (base == end). Both still stand beside the tree, so `unsettled_stop` stops dispatch and integration over them before any move runs. If the drive's next step is integration over a reusable stored green (gate_step skipped, so no advance_member), the stop names `restore`, restore refuses and points at a move, and the next `next` stops again, with no verb that gets out. `_resume` already settles both shapes by dropping the copy.
findings.resolution: In restore_copy, settle both shapes the way `_resume` does: drop the copy (`_drop_copy`) when it has no index.json, or when base == end and `_newer_work` names nothing. Return restored=None with what was dropped instead of a refusal. Add a case for the recorded-move copy, which the executor lists as untested.

preExisting.issue: After any cleanup removal, `git worktree prune` deletes every admin directory whose tree directory is gone. That includes one holding a move's copy, which `unsettled_stop` deliberately does not stop on for a missing directory (drive-phase.py:4822).
preExisting.resolution: Before pruning, list the prunable records and skip, or name, any whose admin directory holds `audit-advance` or its tombstone.
